name: Mokpe / Mòkpè
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Atindogbe, Gratien. 2013. A grammatical sketch of Mòkpè (Bakweri), Bantu A20. African Study Monographs, Supplementary Issue 45: 1-163. Kyoto: Center for African Area Studies, Kyoto University. hdl 2433/171629 (repository PDF).
catalog_locator: Part II Phonology, sec. 3 'Tones', 3.1 'Lexical tones' and 3.2 'Grammatical tones', p. 11; cf. sec. 5 'Syllable Structure', p. 14.
catalog_quote: 3. Tones 1. Lexical tones Like most Bantu languages of the zone, Mokpe contrasts two lexical basic tones: the low (`) and the high (´). However, a downstepped high tone (ꜝ́), the falling (ˆ) and the rising (ˇ) are equally noted. The falling and the rising are the results of the combination of the two basic tones. Example: Low: ŋmà "year", wɔ̀kpɔ̀ "beard", lìkpàmbà "cassava"; High: kɔ́ "snail", ɲáŋgá "sand", ímbúndá "friends"; Falling: lìβê "breast (female)", ɲô "body"; Rising: tǔ "room", lìmě "to swallow", mɔ̌lèŋgù "sheep" 2. Grammatical tones The language equally exhibits grammatical tones. This is illustrated in the paired phrases in (8), where the indefinite and definite articles are rendered by the low and the high tone respectively. mòtò / βàtò cl. 1/2 "a man / people"; mótò / βátò "the man / the people" ... wòzrô cl. 14 "a face"; wôzrô "the face" [p. 14, sec. 5] Mokpe has two syllabic shapes: CV and V. The most common shape is CV.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mokpwe is described as a two-tone (L, H) Bantu language with derived contour tones and downstep, lexical and grammatical tone functions, CV/V syllables; the sketch gives no role to word stress or accent and never mentions either. Corroborated by Monikang 1989 (ch. 5, pp. 66-80: prosody = vowel length + tone; p. 92 'Mokpwe is a language with four tones (high, low, rising, and falling)') and Kagaya 1992 (sec. 2-3: L and H contrastive underlyingly), none of which states a stress position or explicitly denies stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes only: downstepped H; word-final L after L realized super-low/falling at the intonational level (Kagaya 1992); Meeussen's Rule lowering the second of two H (Atindogbe 2013 pp. 20-21).
new_statements.domain_note: All statements concern lexical/grammatical tone on words in citation form and short phrases; no source distinguishes word-level from phrase-level prominence or discusses stress at any level. Absence of a stress statement is an argument from silence across three independent phonological descriptions (1989, 1992, 2013), not an explicit 'no stress' claim.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the same language (Glottolog mokp1239, ISO bri; names Mokpwe/Mokpe/Mòkpè/Bakweri/Bakwiri/Bakueri/Kpe, Guthrie A22). Atindogbe 2013 is based on Buea-area speech; Kagaya's informants are from Voba and Bonakanda villages near Buea; Monikang 1989 is a University of Yaounde diploma dissertation on 'Mokpwe' (MPG record also tags bwt Bafaw-Balong, but the thesis itself is on Mokpwe/Bakweri only). No dialect-level glottocodes involved.

tone_statements.citation: Marlo, Michael R. & David Odden. 2014. Bakweri tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 295-312.
tone_statements.quote: the surface long vowels and contours derive from morphologically concatenating distinct H‑ and L‑toned vowels ... Specified Ls play a role in the tonology of Bakweri. A final Ø vs. L contrast underlies the difference between tenses which acquire H before another word versus those which do not. Other contrasting final melodies are H, LH, and HL. Floating L triggers downstep of a following H ... Bakweri verbs fall into two lexical tone classes, / H/ and / L/. The lexical tone is realized on the first vowel, and subsequent tones are determined by inflectional and phrasal melodic tones.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 296-297, sect. 1 Introduction (under 'p.296 ') and sect. 2.1 Basic pattern (under 'p.297 ')
tone_statements.summary: Verb tone analysed with H and L (plus toneless vowels): lexical H/L on the root's first vowel, tense melodies L, Ø, H, HL, LH on the final vowel; floating L causes downstep; contours = H+L sequences.

tone_statements.quote: Tonal patterns of the Bakueri nouns in the isolation form are classified into 13 types. ... (1) in some types of underlying representations, a tone bearing unit (TBU) should be marked with “*”, which specifies the position associated with the initial tone of the basic tones (BT), ant (2) four types of basic tone(s), i-e., L, H, LH and HL, should be set up. ... The downstep phenomenon is also observed in this language, but it is a free variant of the rising (i.e., LH) tone.
tone_statements.summary: Noun tone: four underlying basic tone melodies L, H, LH, HL (built of level H and L), each of two types adding a free H or a free L; 13 surface patterns; downstep = free variant of rising LH.

tone_statements.citation: Hawkinson, Ann Katherine. 1986. Bakweri verb morphology. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. xviii+287 pp. (Ann Arbor: UMI)
tone_statements.quote: Bakweri is a tone language where different syllables are pronounced at different steady state pitch levels. Contour tones exist only as aresult of two tones combining to form a rising or falling tone;examples are given in 3.4.2:37. Pnonemically, it has three phonemic tones: high, low and a downstepped high tone. The phonemic status of the downstepped high tone is problematic because in many occurrences it can be derived from a sequence of low and high tones) cf. 3.4.4: 40. However, there are enough instances where its presence cannot be explained ... for it to merit phonemic status.
tone_statements.summary: Three phonemic tones: high, low, downstepped high; rising/falling are H+L, L+H from vowel coalescence, not phonemic; each syllable carries a tone; downdrift; floating low tones (cl. 9/10 prefix).

sources.quote: Bakweri has five "basic" tonemes [...]: High H; Low L; Falling HL; Rising LH; Downstep-High 'H. There are, in addition, several "complex" tones (rising-falling, falling-rising) which are rare and highly constrained; they will be ignored. [...] The tones as given here are taxonomic phonemic in intent [...]. The contour tones bear a much lighter functional load in the language than do the level H and L tones, and usually arise as combinations of underlying H and L tones.
sources.note: Five 'basic' taxonomic-phonemic tonemes H, L, falling HL, rising LH and downstepped H, plus rare complex contours; contours carry light functional load and arise from underlying H+L combinations; distinguishes phonological downstep (from downdrift over H-L-H, target underlyingly L) from grammatical downstep (target underlyingly H, part of the morphotonological contour of many constructions, e.g. negative tenses), then reanalyses grammatical downstep as a floating L tone and uses it for internal reconstruction of the polar-toned negative morpheme za.

sources.note: Treats Bakwiri as a tone language whose tone pattern is a property of the whole word (tones stay in place when syllables are swapped in a word game); gives no tone inventory or count.

tone.quote: the tone pattern of disyllabic words in Bakwiri is not affected by the word game transformation. These patterns are shown in a systematic fashion in (10). ... As was true for the length pattern of words, speakers abstract the tone pattern as a property of the whole word, that is, without a particular tone being attached to a particular syllable or segment. This suggests that in Bakwiri tone is a suprasegmental feature. ... I conclude, then, that there is strong evidence that the word is the tone-bearing unit in the African tone languages
